title: There Are 2 Eclipses This August. Here’s How to See Them
gist: WIRED's viewing guide to the only two remaining eclipses of 2026: a total solar eclipse on August 12 whose land totality touches eastern Greenland, western Iceland and Spain — the Iberian Peninsula's first in over a century, at sunset with ~2 minutes of totality — and a near-total partial lunar eclipse on August 27–28 covering up to 96 percent of the lunar disk, best seen across the Americas.

themes.theme: August 12 total solar eclipse and its path

insights.claim: A total solar eclipse occurs on August 12, 2026, with the moon's shadow tracking west to east from the Arctic and delivering partial views to Alaska, Canada, Iceland, parts of the North Atlantic, parts of Europe and the eastern US.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: A broad partial-visibility footprint across North America and Europe means a large addressable audience for eclipse-glasses, travel and streaming demand spikes.

insights.claim: Totality on August 12 touches land only in sparsely populated eastern Greenland, the far western edge of Iceland, and Spain — the most populated region in the path.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Spain concentrates essentially all of the eclipse-tourism demand for this event; hotel, transport and viewing-equipment demand there is the tradable expression.
insights.quote: Sparsely populated stretches of eastern Greenland will see the sun completely obscured, as will the far western edge of Iceland. Spain is the most populated region in the path of totality.
insights.locator: Only a few areas on land will get to see totality

insights.claim: This is the first total solar eclipse over the Iberian Peninsula in more than a century, making it a once-in-generations domestic event for Spain.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Century-scale rarity drives outsized one-off spending and media attention — the kind of event that shifts a quarter of regional tourism receipts.
insights.quote: It’s the first time the Iberian Peninsula will be treated to a full solar eclipse in more than a century.
insights.locator: Spain is the most populated region in the path of totality

insights.claim: In almost all of Spain the August 12 eclipse coincides with sunset, with totality around 8:30 pm Central European Time, the full event lasting about an hour and totality about two minutes.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: A low-horizon sunset totality is the visually dramatic scenario that maximizes viewing turnout and imagery — plan logistics for a two-minute window.
insights.quote: Times vary slightly by city, but in almost all of Spain the eclipse will occur at sunset, with totality around 8:30 pm Central European Time.

insights.claim: The partial lunar eclipse of August 27–28 will place up to 96 percent of the lunar disk in Earth's shadow, making it visually close to a total eclipse.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: A near-total 96 percent obscuration is the rare 'partial' worth planning for; expect total-eclipse-level public interest.
insights.quote: While the eclipse is partial, up to 96 percent of the lunar disk will be in the Earth’s shadow, making for a dramatic view.

insights.claim: Unlike a solar eclipse, the lunar eclipse is visible simultaneously across a vast region, best seen across the Americas — eastern and central Canada, the US, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and South America.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Wide simultaneous visibility means no travel required — the accessible event of the two, with viewing quality gated by light pollution rather than geography.
insights.quote: Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse does not follow a narrow path across the Earth.

insights.claim: In Mexico City the partial phase begins at 8:30 pm local time on August 27, peaks around 10:13 pm and ends at 11:53 pm.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Concrete local timing anchors the viewing window for the largest metro in the prime visibility zone.
insights.locator: How to view it: In the Americas

insights.claim: The 2026 astronomical calendar contains only four eclipses in total, and the two August events are the last of the year because the other two have already occurred.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: No further eclipse catalysts in 2026 after August — any eclipse-linked demand pulls forward into this month.
insights.quote: The 2026 astronomical calendar features only four eclipses. But August is a bounty of riches, with two set to occur.
insights.locator: The 2026 astronomical calendar features only four eclipses

insights.claim: Solar eclipse viewing must never be done with the naked eye, a warning the piece repeats twice, while lunar viewing requires only clear skies and distance from city light pollution.
insights.speaker: Javier Carbajal
insights.so_what: Eye-safety requirements are what create the recurring pre-eclipse surge in certified solar-filter and eclipse-glasses sales.
insights.quote: How to view it: For one, not with your naked eye!
insights.locator: How to view it: For one, not with your naked eye
